newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar hit by ringgit demand,thin market.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar hit by ringgit demand,thin market.

text.p: Flush money market liquidity, thin trading conditions and the Malaysian ringgit's return to favour combined to drag down the Singapore dollar against its U.S. counterpart on Tuesday, forex dealers said.
The Singapore dollar was quoted at S$1.4160/70 to the dollar in late Asian trade after hitting a low of S$1.4165 against its opening below S$1.4100.
A U.S. bank dealer said the Singapore dollar's decline was sparked by a New York-based fund buying into the ringgit/Sing cross in early trade, lifting the rate from an opening 0.5660/65.
"I think it was just people going into carry trades again because if you short dollars against the ringgit, you can make on the swap points," he said.
He said the original move seemed to be driven by funds establishing new positions but it had caused other players to follow suit.
Ringgit/Sing was quoted at 0.5685/91 in late afternoon trade, close to its target of 0.5700, not seen since July 1996.
He said the U.S. dollar faced a temporary top around the S$1.4165/70 level, but it could easily reach S$1.4200 within the week.
Dealers said the Singapore dollar's slide was exaggerated by thin market conditions and stop-loss U.S. dollar buying above S$1.4130.

"Also liquidity's been very flush today because funds have returned to the system over the holidays so that's undermined some support for the Sing dollar," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International.

Dealers said there was no indication of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, despite the domestic unit's relatively steep fall, partly because it was in line with the U.S. dollar's strength against major currencies.

They said the market had also gone short on the U.S. dollar before a four-day break to mark the Chinese and Moslem new years on expectations the Singapore dollar would gain sharply as it did during the same period last year.

"There was a lot of talk that there'd be a big sell-off in dollar/Sing like the year before. So I think a lot of people squared up their positions ahead of that. Now they're just getting back in and going short Sing, long a high-yielding currency such as the ringgit," said a chief dealer at a Hong Kong-based bank.
